payloadSchema.title: Chat — Direct message — payload
payloadSchema.description: One person writes, rewrites or withdraws a message, or a reaction, in their direct conversation with another. A message is named by its author-minted `messageId` and carries its whole content on every revision; the author edits it by sending the same `messageId` with a greater `revision` and an `editedAt`, withdraws it by sending a rewrite with an empty `body`, and reacts to another message with a message of `kind: reaction` whose `body` is the reaction's value. The content vocabulary is the rooms one (`rooms/_shared/0.1`, `SealedRecordBody`). The outer document members (id, type, issuer, recipient, issuedAt, expiresAt, proof) are owned by the framework — SPEC §6.3.

kind.description: What a reader shows the message as: `message`, a turn in the conversation, or `reaction`, a short response to another message. REQUIRED here, where rooms makes it optional only for readers that predate it. An open set: a reader MUST present a kind it does not know as rooms says (as a note, its `body` inert) and MUST NOT refuse a document for its kind. A rewrite MUST keep it.

inReplyTo.description: OPTIONAL on a `message`: the message this one answers. REQUIRED on a `reaction`: the message it responds to, which a rewrite of the reaction MUST keep.

writtenAt.description: The instant the author wrote the message, RFC 3339 in UTC (`Z`). REQUIRED. Set on revision 1 and carried unchanged on every rewrite; what marks an edit is `editedAt`. The author's claim: a reader orders the conversation by it and treats an implausible or backdated one as the specification's *Ordering in the conversation* says.

editedAt.description: The instant the author made the edit that produced this revision, RFC 3339 in UTC (`Z`). Absent on revision 1 and REQUIRED on every later revision, so a reader seeing a message for the first time can tell whether it was edited. Display only: it never orders rewrites.

oneOf.description: The first revision of a message or reaction: `revision` 1, a non-empty `body`, no `editedAt`, and a reaction names its target in `inReplyTo`.

revision.description: Revision 1: the first time the author sends this `messageId`.

body.description: The message's content, which a first revision MUST NOT leave empty: only a rewrite withdraws a message by emptying its `body`.

kind.description: A reaction, which MUST name the message it responds to in `inReplyTo`; matching this subschema refuses a reaction without one.

oneOf.description: A rewrite (an edit, a withdrawal, a changed or withdrawn reaction): `revision` greater than 1, `editedAt` present, and a reaction names its target in `inReplyTo`.

revision.description: A revision greater than 1: a rewrite of a message the author sent before under the same `messageId`.

kind.description: A reaction, which MUST name the message it responds to in `inReplyTo`; matching this subschema refuses a reaction without one.

Ext.title: Ext
Ext.description: Vendor-namespaced extension object per SPEC.md §4.5.1. Each immediate key MUST be a reverse-DNS namespace; structure under each namespace is opaque to the framework.

RecordEditedAt.title: RecordEditedAt
RecordEditedAt.description: The instant the author made the edit that produced this version, RFC 3339 in UTC (`Z`). Set by the writer of every version after the first, and absent on the first, so that a reader seeing a record for the first time can tell whether it was ever edited — which `version` cannot say, since curation moves it too. Signed with the body on the sealed tiers. A reader shows a record carrying it as edited, and treats an implausible one as `SealedRecordBody` (*Edits*) says. Governed by `RoomProfile.recordMembers` like `writtenAt`. No host enforces or reads it.

RecordWrittenAt.title: RecordWrittenAt
RecordWrittenAt.description: The instant the author wrote the record, RFC 3339 in UTC (`Z`). Set by the author and kept unchanged when the record is rewritten; an edit is marked by `editedAt`. OPTIONAL on a note; a `message` or `reaction` SHOULD carry it. The author's claim, not an attested time: a reader orders messages by it, compares it with the host's `createdAt`, and treats an implausible or backdated one as `SealedRecordBody` (*When it was written*) says. No host enforces or reads it.

MessageReference.title: MessageReference
MessageReference.description: Names another message of the same direct conversation: the message a reply answers, or the message a reaction responds to. Never a message of another conversation. A reader resolves it only against messages it already holds for this conversation and MUST NOT fetch anything because of it. It MUST NOT name a message of kind `reaction`. The counterpart of the rooms `RecordReference`, with `messageId` in place of `key`.

MessageId.title: MessageId
MessageId.description: Names one message, or one reaction, across all of its revisions: 32 random bytes, base64url without padding (43 characters), the same convention as the rooms `FileManifest.fileId`. Minted by the message's author for its first revision and carried unchanged on every rewrite. It MUST be fresh and unguessable and MUST NOT be derived from the content, the counterparty, the time or any other identifier (SPEC §13.1 item 2). It is not the document `id`: a document `id` is used once per document, while a `messageId` names one message across every document that writes it. Opaque: a reader MUST NOT read meaning into it.

MessageBody.title: MessageBody
MessageBody.description: The words of the message. On `kind: message`, plain text: a reader MUST NOT render it as markup (not markdown, not HTML, not a link it follows) and never follows a URL in it by itself. On `kind: reaction`, the reaction's value: normalised to NFC with every U+FE0E and U+FE0F removed before it is measured or compared, at most 64 code points after that normalisation, and one line (no U+000A, U+000B, U+000C, U+000D, U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029), as the rooms *A reaction's value* rule says. Empty means the message or reaction is withdrawn, which only a rewrite (`revision` greater than 1) may say.

RecordKind.title: RecordKind
RecordKind.description: What a reader shows a record as. Defined values: `note` — something kept in the room's library, titled or not, its `body` markdown; `message` — a turn in the room's conversation, its words in `body` as plain text; `reaction` — a short response to another record, its value in `body` (`SealedRecordBody`, *Reactions*). An open set, not an enumeration, so a new kind needs no new version of any schema: a reader MUST present a record whose kind it does not know as a note, and MUST NOT refuse a record for its kind. Absent means `note`, though a reader that keeps a conversation apart MAY show an untitled record without a kind as a message (*Untitled records*). A new version of a record MUST keep its kind. lowerCamelCase, at most 64 characters.

MessageRevision.title: MessageRevision
MessageRevision.description: The author's revision number for a `messageId`: `1` on the first document written for it, and a strictly greater integer on each rewrite. Gaps are allowed, since every revision carries the whole message. The only key a reader orders rewrites by; `editedAt` never orders. Never shown.

Unknown top-level member — additionalProperties: false catches `queue`, which a caller might add expecting to scope the delete; msgIds already identify the messages across both queues.
Empty msgIds — a status request naming nothing is malformed, not an empty answer; minItems: 1 catches it.
More than 100 msgIds — the per-request cap bounds the lookups one document can cause; maxItems: 100 catches it.
Duplicate msgIds — statuses are one-per-id in request order, so a duplicate adds nothing and makes the pairing ambiguous; uniqueItems catches it.
Empty-string msgId — minLength: 1 on each item; an empty handle can never name a stored message.
A `did` naming another account — this task answers only for the requester's own sent messages, so there is no `did` member; additionalProperties: false catches it.
Empty msgIds — a status request naming nothing is malformed, not an empty answer; minItems: 1 catches it.

0.1's `statuses[].at` does not exist in 0.2; it is `reachedAt`.
Membership event with an unknown change.
Membership event carrying a scope — membership events are metadata about who rides a connection, not what they may do there.
Membership event without a reason.
A wire that is not a mux wire — the subprotocol name is not the value.

seq.description: Batch sequence number, starting at 1 and increasing by exactly 1 per batch within a subscription. A gap means batches were lost in transit.

events.description: Traffic events in the order the mediator observed them. May be empty on a heartbeat batch, and is always empty on a subscription that turned traffic events off.

dropped.description: Traffic events that matched the filter but were discarded since the previous batch — rate ceiling exceeded or subscriber not connected. Membership events are counted in `membershipDropped`, never here.

expiresAt.description: The subscription's current expiry, so the subscriber can renew before it lapses.

membership.description: Mux membership events, in the order the mediator observed them. Present only on a subscription that opted in to them with messaging/monitor/subscribe `membership`, and then on every batch, empty when there is nothing to report.

membershipDropped.description: Membership events that matched the subscription's membership filter but were discarded since the previous batch. Present exactly when `membership` is.

Ext.description: Vendor-namespaced extension object per SPEC.md §4.5.1. Each immediate key MUST be a reverse-DNS namespace; structure under each namespace is opaque to the framework.

MonitorMembershipEvent.title: MonitorMembershipEvent
MonitorMembershipEvent.description: One change to the membership of one mux connection at the mediator: a member DID attached to or detached from a principal's connection. Not a step in the life of a message, so it is not a MonitorEvent and carries none of its members. Carries metadata only — never a message, a signed statement, a nonce or key material.

occurredAt.description: When the change took effect, with sub-second precision where the mediator has it.

principal.description: The DID the connection is authenticated as, in the same form the mediator uses for accounts.

member.description: The member DID that attached or detached, in the same form the mediator uses for accounts.

source.description: Whether the member rides, or rode, the connection through a stored grant or a session attach.

reason.description: Why, exactly as the messaging/mux/event entry for the change reports it: an AttachReason value when `change` is `attached`, a DetachReason value when it is `detached`.

sessionId.description: The connection's identifier, as its `ready` event announced it and messaging/mux/connections lists it. Absent when the mediator does not report it.

MembershipChange.title: MembershipChange
MembershipChange.description: What happened to a member DID's place on a mux connection, as messaging/mux/event reports it to the connection's principal. `attached`: the member joined the connection, or its scope or expiry there changed. `detached`: the member left the connection, or a stored grant of it was not attached on connect.

SessionId.title: SessionId
SessionId.description: The mediator's identifier for one authenticated connection, as announced in that connection's `ready` event.

MemberChangeReason.title: MemberChangeReason
MemberChangeReason.description: The reason carried by one member's change in a messaging/mux/event `attached` or `detached` event: exactly the AttachReason values followed by the DetachReason values, with their meanings. An `attached` event carries only AttachReason values and a `detached` event only DetachReason values. One closed set rather than a union, so every generated binding types it as one enumeration; it MUST be kept equal to the two sets it joins.

MuxSource.title: MuxSource
MuxSource.description: How a member came to be on a connection: through a stored grant, or through a session attach bound to that connection.

MuxWire.title: MuxWire
MuxWire.description: The wire a mux connection speaks: `didcomm`, a DIDComm WebSocket that negotiated the `didcomm-mux` subprotocol; `tsp`, a raw-TSP WebSocket that negotiated `tsp-mux`. The same values messaging/mux/connections reports for a connection's `wire`.

Vid.title: Vid
Vid.description: A Verifiable Identifier (SPEC §4.8). For a mediator-served account this is the account's controlling DID, carried verbatim and compared by exact string equality. For privacy — and because some mediators key accounts by a one-way hash and never hold the full DID — a stable hash of the DID (e.g. its SHA-256 digest) is an equally valid value here: producer and consumer simply agree on the same opaque identifier and compare by exact string equality. The field carries whichever form the issuing mediator uses.

MonitorEvent.title: MonitorEvent
MonitorEvent.description: One observed step in the life of one message at the mediator. Carries metadata only — never a message body.

occurredAt.description: When the step happened, with sub-second precision where the mediator has it.

msgId.description: The stored message's identifier, once it has one; correlates the events of one message and matches MessageMeta.msgId.

from.description: The sender, where the mediator knows it.

to.description: The recipient, where the mediator knows it.

messageType.description: The plaintext message type, present only when the mediator itself was the addressee and read it (a routing forward, a pickup request, a trust-task type URI, a trust ping). Absent for end-to-end-encrypted traffic the mediator only relays.

outcome.description: Present when stage is `refused`, and on any other stage that failed.

latencyMs.description: For `delivered` and `forwarded`: milliseconds since the message was stored.

TrafficOutcome.title: TrafficOutcome
TrafficOutcome.description: Why a frame was refused or failed.

code.description: The stable error code the mediator returned to the sender (a trust-task-error or problem-report code).

WireProtocol.title: WireProtocol
WireProtocol.description: The protocol a message travelled in, as the mediator detected it from the wire form. `didcomm` is DIDComm v2 (JWE/JWS); `didcommV1` is a DIDComm v1 envelope; `tsp` is a Trust Spanning Protocol message; `other` is anything the mediator could not classify.

TrafficChannel.title: TrafficChannel
TrafficChannel.description: How the traffic reached or left the mediator. `peerMediator` is mediator-to-mediator forwarding.

TrafficStage.title: TrafficStage
TrafficStage.description: What happened. `received`: a frame arrived. `stored`: it was queued for a local account. `delivered`: handed to its recipient. `forwarded`: relayed to another mediator. `refused`: rejected (see the event's `outcome`). `deleted`: removed by its recipient or an administrator. `expired`: removed by expiry. `purged`: removed by a queue purge.

TrafficDirection.title: TrafficDirection
TrafficDirection.description: `inbound`: arriving at the mediator. `outbound`: leaving it (delivery to a recipient, or a forward to another mediator). `internal`: a state change with no wire traffic (expiry, deletion, purge).

payloadSchema.title: Messaging — Subscribe to Traffic Monitor — payload

filter.description: Selects the traffic events the subscription receives. Absent or empty selects every traffic event the requester is entitled to see.

leaseSeconds.description: How long the subscription lives unless renewed. Default 300.

maxEventsPerSecond.description: Rate ceiling the subscriber can absorb; the mediator MAY apply a lower one. Events over the ceiling are counted as dropped, never queued.

subscriptionId.description: Renew or re-filter an existing subscription held by the same requester. Omitted = create a new one.

traffic.description: False turns traffic events off, so that the subscription receives only the membership events it opts in to; `filter` MUST then be absent. Absent or true keeps them on, as in 0.1.

membership.description: Opts the subscription in to mux membership events and selects which. Absent: no membership events — they are never sent by default.

filter.description: The filter in force, after the mediator narrowed it to what the requester is entitled to see.

traffic.description: Present and false exactly when the subscription receives no traffic events.

membership.description: The membership filter in force, after the mediator narrowed it to what the requester is entitled to see. Absent when the subscription receives no membership events — because none were asked for, or because the mediator does not offer them (mux not enabled, or a mediator implementing only 0.1).

payloadSchema.title: Messaging — Mux Admin List — payload
payloadSchema.description: An administrator lists the stored mux grants of a principal DID, of a member DID, or between the two, a page at a time, without their signed statements. The outer document members are owned by the framework — SPEC §6.3.

principal.description: Only grants delegated to this principal DID. At least one of `principal` and `member` is REQUIRED.

member.description: Only grants on this member DID; the response then carries the member's current `epoch`. At least one of `principal` and `member` is REQUIRED.

cursor.description: An opaque continuation token from a previous response's `nextCursor`, bound to the requester and the other request members; a responder MUST NOT accept a cursor it did not issue.

limit.description: The most grants to return, at most 500; the responder chooses a default (100) and MAY return fewer.

AdminGrantView.title: AdminGrantView
AdminGrantView.description: An administrator's view of one stored grant: what it delegates, to whom, in what state and until when. Unlike GrantView, never the signed statement — that goes only to the grant's two parties, through messaging/mux/list.

principal.description: The principal DID the grant delegates to.

scope.description: The effective scope: the signed scope, or the narrower one messaging/mux/update set.

expiresAt.description: The effective expiry: the signed `exp` rendered as RFC 3339, or the earlier one messaging/mux/update set.

epoch.description: The member DID's epoch the grant was signed under. A grant whose epoch is earlier than the member's current one is dead (`epochRevoked`).

signedAt.description: The statement's signed `iat`, rendered as RFC 3339.

narrowed.description: True when messaging/mux/update narrowed the effective scope or expiry below what the statement signs.

Response.title: Messaging — Mux Admin List — response payload
Response.description: The success response to a messaging/mux/admin-list request. Carried in a Trust Task document whose type is https://trusttasks.org/spec/messaging/mux/admin-list/0.1#response.

grants.description: Grants in every state, active and dead ones still within the retention window, ordered by member DID, then principal DID, then grant identifier.

epoch.description: Present exactly when the request named `member`: that member DID's current epoch, which messaging/mux/admin-revoke-all names to advance it.

nextCursor.description: Continuation token for the next page; pass it back as `cursor`. Absent on the last page — never `null`.

MuxScope.title: MuxScope
MuxScope.description: A set of capabilities: a non-empty JSON array of MuxScopeValue, compared as a set — order is not significant and a repeated value collapses into one. Never empty: an empty scope is refused, never read as "all". There is no default scope anywhere — every attach and every grant names its scope explicitly. A scope is always bounded by the member DID's own access-control capabilities at the mediator.

MuxScopeValue.title: MuxScopeValue
MuxScopeValue.description: One capability a member DID extends to a principal's connection. `receive`: live delivery of the member's inbound messages on the connection. `pickup`: message-pickup status and delivery requests naming the member as `recipient_did`, and inclusion in a raw-TSP inbox drain. `delete`: deleting the member's stored messages, including delete-on-ack and delete-on-send; a member without `delete` keeps its messages in its inbox until something holding `delete` collects them. `send`: the mediator accepts on this connection frames whose sender is the member DID — the frame is still signed or authcrypted with the member's own keys; the scope only lets the mediator accept it on this socket.

GrantState.title: GrantState
GrantState.description: A stored grant's state. `active`: valid; the member is attached whenever the principal is connected. `suspended`: the member DID proved control with a key that signed none of its active grants (the unknown-key rule); terminal — the grant cannot be resumed and must be recreated by a fresh member signature. `staleKey`: the key that signed the grant is no longer in the member DID's current authentication relationship; terminal — it does not become active again if the key reappears. `expired`: an active grant past its effective expiry; computed when read, never stored. `epochRevoked`: the member DID advanced its epoch with messaging/mux/revoke-all. A grant revoked with messaging/mux/revoke has no state: it is deleted. A dead grant (every state but `active`) stays listable for the mediator's retention window after its effective expiry, then is pruned.

MuxDid.title: MuxDid
MuxDid.description: A DID, carried verbatim and compared by exact string equality. Unlike the messaging family's `Vid`, never a hash: the mediator resolves it to verify a statement signed by it. For a member DID reached over TSP, the TSP VID is the DID itself.

GrantId.title: GrantId
GrantId.description: A grant's identifier, chosen by the member DID's signer and carried in its grant statement; a UUID is RECOMMENDED. A mediator refuses a grant whose identifier is already on the member DID's record.

AdminGrantView.title: AdminGrantView
AdminGrantView.description: An administrator's view of one stored grant: what it delegates, to whom, in what state and until when. Unlike GrantView, never the signed statement — that goes only to the grant's two parties, through messaging/mux/list.

principal.description: The principal DID the grant delegates to.

scope.description: The effective scope: the signed scope, or the narrower one messaging/mux/update set.

signedAt.description: The statement's signed `iat`, rendered as RFC 3339.

narrowed.description: True when messaging/mux/update narrowed the effective scope or expiry below what the statement signs.

payloadSchema.title: Messaging — Mux Admin Revoke — payload
payloadSchema.description: An administrator revokes stored mux grants of other accounts — those of a principal DID, of a member DID, or between the two, optionally narrowed to named grant identifiers — a bounded batch at a time. The outer document members are owned by the framework — SPEC §6.3.

principal.description: Only grants delegated to this principal DID. At least one of `principal` and `member` is REQUIRED.

member.description: Only grants on this member DID. At least one of `principal` and `member` is REQUIRED.

grantIds.description: With `member` only: only these grants of the member DID. A grant identifier is unique on its member's record alone, so it is never accepted without `member`.

payloadSchema.title: Messaging — Wake Request — payload
payloadSchema.description: A sender that has just queued mail for a DID asks that DID's mediator to ring the device, naming the queued messages by the identifiers the mediator stores them under. Contentless: no task type, reason or content. The mediator answers every request with the same empty response, whatever it did.

addressee.description: The DID the queued messages are addressed to — an account at the mediator receiving this request.

msgIds.description: The messages the requester queued for the addressee, by the identifier the addressee's mediator stores each under (as messaging/message/status and messaging/message/list name them). Holding one is evidence of having held the stored message.

urgency.description: OPTIONAL. Passed to the gateway as push/wake's urgency hint. `interactive`: a person is expected to act now. `background`: the device may collect at its convenience. Absent: the mediator sends no urgency.

ext.description: Ecosystem-defined extension members per SPEC.md §4.5.1. A mediator ignores every ext member when deciding whether to ring.

payloadSchema.title: Messaging — Wake Set — payload
payloadSchema.description: An account gives its own mediator the opaque wake handle its push gateway issued for it, or takes it back, so that the mediator can ring the account's device when a sender asks it to (messaging/wake/request). The mediator never receives a platform push token. Absence of `wakeHandle` clears the handle.

wakeHandle.description: The opaque handle the account's push gateway issued at push/register, with the gateway that acts on it. Present: replaces whatever handle the mediator held for this account. Absent: the mediator drops the handle it held, and the account is no longer wakeable through this mediator.

wakeCapable.description: true when the mediator now holds a handle for the account and will ask the handle's gateway to ring on a qualifying messaging/wake/request. false when it holds none — the request cleared it, or the mediator does not ring for this account (its operator does not offer waking, or it cannot reach the named gateway over any transport it speaks).

WakeHandle.title: WakeHandle
WakeHandle.description: An opaque, gateway-issued reference to a device's push channel (push wake-up binding, https://trusttasks.org/binding/push/0.1). The push gateway returns it to the device at registration; the device conveys it to its VTA (device/set-wake), and the VTA provisions it to authorized triggers (its mediator and/or itself). The raw platform push token (APNs/FCM/WebPush) is held ONLY by the gateway and is never represented here — the handle abstracts the platform, so adding new push methods (e.g. PWA Web Push) needs no change to triggers or VTA config. A handle is a bearer capability to *request* a wake (subject to the gateway's allowlist), never to read the channel.

gateway.description: The push gateway that issued this handle and acts on it — a DID (DIDComm-reachable gateway) or an https URL (REST gateway). A trigger sends its contentless wake request here.

handle.description: Opaque gateway-issued identifier for the device's push channel. Reveals no platform token. Rotates whenever the device re-registers a new platform token with the gateway; the device then re-conveys the fresh handle via device/set-wake.

payloadSchema.title: Push Register — payload
payloadSchema.description: A device registers its platform push token (APNs / FCM / Web Push) with a push gateway and names who controls the resulting handle's trigger allowlist: a controller VTA (`controllerVtaDid`), or — where the gateway's policy admits it — the device itself (`selfControl`), with its own initial allowlist. Exactly one of the two. The gateway returns an opaque WakeHandle; the raw token is held by the gateway only. See the push wake-up binding (https://trusttasks.org/binding/push/0.1).

registration.description: The platform push channel (token). Held by the gateway only — never disclosed to any other party.

controllerVtaDid.description: The DID of the VTA permitted to provision this handle's trigger allowlist (push/provision). The device conveys the resulting handle to this VTA via device/set-wake. Absent when `selfControl` is present.

selfControl.description: The device controls this handle itself: the gateway records the registering device's authenticated DID as the controller and starts the handle with the allowlist given here. Admitted only where the gateway's policy allows self-controlled handles. Absent when `controllerVtaDid` is present.

SelfControl.title: SelfControl
SelfControl.description: A self-controlled handle's initial trigger allowlist. The device names the parties it allows to wake it — typically its own mediator, the only party that knows when mail is queued for it and it is offline.

allowedTriggers.description: DIDs permitted to trigger a wake for this handle. Empty: nobody, until the device provisions a list (push/provision). The device MUST NOT name itself.

wakeHandle.description: The opaque gateway-issued handle (gateway address + handle). Conveyed onward; reveals no token.

Ext.title: Ext
Ext.description: Vendor-namespaced extension object per SPEC.md §4.5.1. Each immediate key MUST be a reverse-DNS namespace; structure under each namespace is opaque to the framework.

WakeHandle.title: WakeHandle
WakeHandle.description: An opaque, gateway-issued reference to a device's push channel (push wake-up binding, https://trusttasks.org/binding/push/0.1). The push gateway returns it to the device at registration; the device conveys it to its VTA (device/set-wake), and the VTA provisions it to authorized triggers (its mediator and/or itself). The raw platform push token (APNs/FCM/WebPush) is held ONLY by the gateway and is never represented here — the handle abstracts the platform, so adding new push methods (e.g. PWA Web Push) needs no change to triggers or VTA config. A handle is a bearer capability to *request* a wake (subject to the gateway's allowlist), never to read the channel.

gateway.description: The push gateway that issued this handle and acts on it — a DID (DIDComm-reachable gateway) or an https URL (REST gateway). A trigger sends its contentless wake request here.

handle.description: Opaque gateway-issued identifier for the device's push channel. Reveals no platform token. Rotates whenever the device re-registers a new platform token with the gateway; the device then re-conveys the fresh handle via device/set-wake.

PushRegistration.title: PushRegistration
PushRegistration.description: A device's platform push channel — the body the device registers with its push GATEWAY (push wake-up binding, https://trusttasks.org/binding/push/0.1; modeled on Aries RFC 0699/0734). The gateway holds this token and returns an opaque WakeHandle in exchange; the token is held by the gateway ONLY, never by the mediator or the maintainer/VTA. The gateway uses it to send a contentless wake-up when an authorized trigger asks — the push payload never carries Trust Task content. Tagged union over the discriminator `platform`.

token.description: APNs device token (hex string issued by Apple Push Notification service).

topic.description: APNs topic — typically the app bundle identifier the gateway pushes to.

environment.description: Which APNs environment issued the token. Maintainers route to the matching APNs endpoint.

token.description: Firebase Cloud Messaging registration token. The gateway sends a data message (not a notification message) so the app controls wake and display.

keys.description: Web Push (RFC 8291) encryption keys. Note: per the push binding the payload remains contentless regardless of this encryption.

A signal delay as a number of milliseconds. The host chooses the interval of a randomised delay; a room chooses only whether there is one, so that no room can pick an interval that marks its writes as plainly as none would.

No presentation. This is the member that carries the room-issued `read` grant, so a payload without it is a request to enumerate a room's key chain with no authority at all — the one omission that must never validate.

fromEpoch below the minimum. Epoch 1 is a room's first and has no predecessor, so there is no rung 1 to return; a request for one is asking for a link that wraps something which is not an earlier epoch's key.

limit of zero. A request that can only ever return nothing is a request whose author meant something else; the floor of 1 makes it say so rather than silently succeeding with an empty chain that reads like a severed history.

Unknown top-level payload member — additionalProperties: false catches `sinceEpoch`. Worth a fixture because it is the plausible wrong guess: the sibling rooms/records/list pages forward with `sinceVersion`, and this task walks backwards with `fromEpoch`.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.
No presentation. The chain is the room's history in wrapped form; it is served on `read` the room conferred, never on an account at the host.
The floor as a string. A key holder compares it with rung numbers to decide what to discard; a string invites one implementation to compare lexically and keep epoch 10 below epoch 9.

An epoch link claiming epoch 1. A room's first epoch has no predecessor, so a rung 1 wraps something that is not an earlier epoch's key; the floor of 2 on EpochLink.epoch is what refuses it. (The stronger rule — that a link's epoch must equal the epoch being minted — is a MUST in prose, because a schema cannot compare two of its own members.)

An epoch link with no nonce. Every rung is AEAD ciphertext and a nonce is not optional for one; a link missing it cannot be opened by anybody, and would be stored as a rung that silently severs the chain at that point.

Unknown member inside the link — additionalProperties: false on EpochLink. A rung carries wrapped key material and nothing descriptive; an extra member is the obvious place to leak what the sealing exists to hide.

Minting epoch 1. An epoch advances by exactly one from an existing room, whose first epoch is 1 already; a request to mint it is either a re-registration or an off-by-one, and both would reset a room rather than advance it.
Bare/unnamespaced ext key — SPEC §4.5.1 requires every immediate child of ext to be reverse-DNS namespaced.

SignalDelay.title: SignalDelay
SignalDelay.description:
Whether a room's host waits a randomised interval before sending a `rooms/changed` signal: the room's **signal delay**.

`randomised` is the default and what a room without one has: the host waits a few seconds after the change that fires a watch, so that the signal's time does not mark one write exactly (`rooms/changed`, producer item 4). `none` is for a room where members expect to see a write as soon as it is made, such as a conversation: the host sends the signal as soon as the change that fires it is stored, with no wait of its own.

**A room's setting, not a member's.** The delay protects the room's writers as much as its watchers. A watcher whose signal is sent at once marks, to anyone who sees both the writer's request reach the host and the signal leave it, the moment of the write and that the two parties share the room. So one watcher cannot opt out for itself without giving away something about everyone who writes, and the setting is the room's: changed by a holder of `admin` (`rooms/signal-delay/set`) and served to every member (`rooms/info`).

**What `none` gives up.** Little in a busy room, where writes are frequent enough that their rhythm is visible anyway; most in a quiet one, where a single write and a single signal line up. A surface that offers the setting SHOULD say so.

Absent means `randomised`.

RecordPrune.title: RecordPrune
RecordPrune.description:
The mark a prune leaves: **that** records were removed, when, and how many — never which, and never anything they said.

A prune removes records outright, tombstones included, so the room's record tree loses leaves and an incremental reader has nothing left to learn the removal from. This is what it learns from instead. A host keeps the latest one per room and serves it with every listing that can carry it (`rooms/records/list` 0.3, as `lastPrune`); a reader whose own copy of the room was synchronised to a version below `version` MUST rebuild that copy from a full listing — no `sinceVersion` — and drop every record the full listing no longer holds. Without that, a record the room removed lives on in every cache that synchronised before the prune, and a record retracted while the reader was away comes back as current.

**What a host keeps and what it does not.** A host keeps this marker, and in its audit trail the prune's `reason`, its requester where the tier discloses one, and the retention it was made under. It MUST NOT keep anything a pruned record said — body, ciphertext, cleartext, title, description, file or blob — and SHOULD NOT keep pruned records' keys: the count is the audit, and a list of keys on an `open` room, where keys may be descriptive, is content by another name.

version.description: The version the prune took from the room's counter, as a put or a curation would. No record carries it; it is what moves `HeadVersion` past the removal, so that a root taken before and a root taken after are never labelled with one version.

removed.description: How many records were removed, tombstones included. A prune that removed nothing leaves no mark.

RecordRetention.title: RecordRetention
RecordRetention.description:
How long a room keeps its records, by age: the room's **record retention**. Records older than it states become **eligible** to be removed by `rooms/records/prune`; nothing is removed until a holder of `admin` asks for a prune, and nothing a prune removes can be brought back.

**Not `retentionPolicy`, and not `retentionDays`.** Both names are taken in this family and mean other things. `retentionPolicy` (`RetentionPolicy`) is whether a room's *key chain* lets a member read epochs from before they joined, fixed at creation because key material either exists for an epoch or it does not. `retentionDays` (`rooms/create`) is how long a host keeps a whole room after it lapses unrenewed. This is a third question — how long the room keeps its *records* while it is live — and unlike the first it is a decision a room revisits, so it is changeable (`rooms/records/retention/set`). A name sharing either's would invite a reader to apply one's rules to the other.

**Age is the host's to measure, so age is `updatedAt`.** On the sealed tiers a host can read nothing of a record but its key, version, status, pinning and when it last changed, so a policy the host applies can only be stated in those terms. That is also why it cannot use a record's own `validUntil`, which is sealed: expiry is a reader's rule, retention a host's. A curation is a change, so it restarts a record's age — a retraction starts a tombstone's.

**Absent, or `{}`, means no record is ever eligible by age**, and that is the reading a host MUST apply whenever it cannot read a policy: removing data under a rule nobody stated is the failure this member exists to prevent. Every member can read the policy in force (`rooms/info`), so a record is never removed under a rule its readers could not have known.

tombstoneDays.description: Days a retracted record's tombstone is kept after its retraction. A tombstone whose `updatedAt` is more than this long ago is eligible. Tombstones exist so that a member syncing incrementally learns of a retraction (`rooms/records/curate`); this is how long a member may stay away and still learn of one that way rather than by rebuilding their copy of the room. Absent means tombstones are never eligible.

recordDays.description: Days a record is kept after it last changed, whatever its standing. A record — `active`, `deprecated` or `retracted` — whose `updatedAt` is more than this long ago is eligible, **unless it is pinned**: pinning says what matters in the room, and a room that wants a pinned record gone unpins it first. Absent means records are never eligible by age.

ext.description: Ecosystem-defined extension members per SPEC.md §4.5.1. A host MUST NOT treat a member here as making more records eligible: a removal rule a member's reader cannot understand is one they were never told about.

RetentionPolicy.title: RetentionPolicy
RetentionPolicy.description: Whether a room keeps its history readable across a membership change, fixed at creation and immutable thereafter — like `Visibility`, and for the same reason: the rungs of an epoch key chain either exist for an epoch or they do not, and no later change of mind can seal key material that was never sealed or unseal what was already severed. `chained`: each advance produces an `EpochLink`, so every member reads the room's whole retained history however long they have been in it — what a **library** wants, at the cost of post-compromise security for record content, since a compromised current key then reaches every retained epoch. `fromJoin`: no rungs are produced, so a member reads only from the epoch their group state is at — what a **stream** wants, and what a room under a strict forward-secrecy obligation wants, at the cost that a joining member finds an empty-looking room and nobody can reread a record once their group state has moved past the epoch it was sealed under. Absent means `chained`; see the prose on why the absent case is the readable one.
RetentionPolicy.$comment: Deliberately no JSON Schema `default`. A declared default is materialised by the generated bindings — the member becomes non-optional with a serde default — so an absent value would reappear as an explicit one on re-serialisation and break round-trip idempotence for every document written before this member existed. The meaning of absence is stated in prose, where a binding cannot act on it.

Visibility.title: Visibility
Visibility.description: How much of a room its host can see, fixed at creation and immutable thereafter. `open`: records are cleartext, searchable and fully audited. `attributed`: record content is sealed, and the host still learns which member acted. `private`: content is sealed and membership is presented in zero knowledge, so the host verifies that a member acted without learning which. Immutable because a downgrade cannot un-see cleartext and an upgrade would protect only what came after while presenting as though it protected everything.

AuthorityPresentation.title: AuthorityPresentation
AuthorityPresentation.description:
What a party presents to act on a room. Carries the whole authority chain: a host MUST NOT dereference an authority credential's `parent` to fetch a link it was not given. Resolving over the network would make verification depend on availability, turn every identifier into a request the host can be induced to make against an address the holder chooses, and signal credential use to whoever hosts the identifier. A host MUST bind the presenter to the chain's leaf. A chain that verifies is evidence that authority was conferred on somebody; it is not evidence that the party presenting it is that somebody. The leaf's subject MUST equal the party the host authenticated for this request — an identity the transport established or a document `proof` proved, never one named in a payload. A host that omits this check authorizes every captured presentation, and the omission is silent, because the chain still verifies.

**Every credential is its issuer's attestation, and only its issuer's.** For the membership credential and for every link of `authority`, a host MUST verify the credential's `proof` with a key that the credential's own `issuer` lists for `assertionMethod` in its DID document, and MUST refuse a credential whose proof names a verification method that is not its issuer's. A proof that verifies under some other party's key is that party's statement, not the issuer's, and confers nothing. The same binding holds for every other document a room signs, such as a `RevocationList`.

**A chain that verifies may still be revoked.** A host that has accepted a `RevocationList` for the room (`rooms/revocations/put`) MUST, from the moment it accepted it, refuse every presentation in which the membership credential or any link of `authority` is revoked by that list, under every task and every version of every task it serves for the room. A chain from which any link is revoked is refused whole: a credential delegated from a revoked one confers nothing, however it was attenuated. The refusal is the same `permissionDenied` as any other failed presentation.

membership.description: The presenter's membership credential for this room, or — on a `private` room — a zero-knowledge presentation of it. Serialized per the governing profile.

authority.description: The authority chain, LEAF FIRST: the first element is the credential being relied on and the last MUST be one issued by the room itself. Every link the presenter relies on is present, because the host will not fetch one. Capped at 8: verification is linear in chain length and runs on every operation, so an unbounded chain is a denial-of-service surface against the host. The known uses need 2 to 3 — a person attenuating to an agent, and that agent to a sub-agent.

subjectBinding.description: REQUIRED on a `private` room, where the subject identifier is withheld: a proof that the membership credential and the authority chain's leaf describe the SAME subject. Without it two parties pool credentials — one contributes membership, the other authority — and the combination verifies as a single party holding both. A host MUST refuse a private-room presentation that omits this.

A declared default is materialised by the generated bindings — the member becomes non-optional with a serde default — so an absent value would reappear as an explicit one on re-serialisation and break round-trip idempotence for every document written before this member existed. The meaning of absence is stated in prose, where a binding cannot act on it.

Visibility.title: Visibility
Visibility.description: How much of a room its host can see, fixed at creation and immutable thereafter. `open`: records are cleartext, searchable and fully audited. `attributed`: record content is sealed, and the host still learns which member acted. `private`: content is sealed and membership is presented in zero knowledge, so the host verifies that a member acted without learning which. Immutable because a downgrade cannot un-see cleartext and an upgrade would protect only what came after while presenting as though it protected everything.

AuthorityPresentation.title: AuthorityPresentation
AuthorityPresentation.description:
What a party presents to act on a room. Carries the whole authority chain: a host MUST NOT dereference an authority credential's `parent` to fetch a link it was not given. Resolving over the network would make verification depend on availability, turn every identifier into a request the host can be induced to make against an address the holder chooses, and signal credential use to whoever hosts the identifier. A host MUST bind the presenter to the chain's leaf. A chain that verifies is evidence that authority was conferred on somebody; it is not evidence that the party presenting it is that somebody. The leaf's subject MUST equal the party the host authenticated for this request — an identity the transport established or a document `proof` proved, never one named in a payload. A host that omits this check authorizes every captured presentation, and the omission is silent, because the chain still verifies.

**Every credential is its issuer's attestation, and only its issuer's.** For the membership credential and for every link of `authority`, a host MUST verify the credential's `proof` with a key that the credential's own `issuer` lists for `assertionMethod` in its DID document, and MUST refuse a credential whose proof names a verification method that is not its issuer's. A proof that verifies under some other party's key is that party's statement, not the issuer's, and confers nothing. The same binding holds for every other document a room signs, such as a `RevocationList`.

**A chain that verifies may still be revoked.** A host that has accepted a `RevocationList` for the room (`rooms/revocations/put`) MUST, from the moment it accepted it, refuse every presentation in which the membership credential or any link of `authority` is revoked by that list, under every task and every version of every task it serves for the room. A chain from which any link is revoked is refused whole: a credential delegated from a revoked one confers nothing, however it was attenuated. The refusal is the same `permissionDenied` as any other failed presentation.

membership.description: The presenter's membership credential for this room, or — on a `private` room — a zero-knowledge presentation of it. Serialized per the governing profile.

authority.description: The authority chain, LEAF FIRST: the first element is the credential being relied on and the last MUST be one issued by the room itself. Every link the presenter relies on is present, because the host will not fetch one. Capped at 8: verification is linear in chain length and runs on every operation, so an unbounded chain is a denial-of-service surface against the host. The known uses need 2 to 3 — a person attenuating to an agent, and that agent to a sub-agent.

subjectBinding.description: REQUIRED on a `private` room, where the subject identifier is withheld: a proof that the membership credential and the authority chain's leaf describe the SAME subject. Without it two parties pool credentials — one contributes membership, the other authority — and the combination verifies as a single party holding both. A host MUST refuse a private-room presentation that omits this.

payloadSchema.title: Rooms Keys Browse — payload
payloadSchema.description: TODO: what the request payload of rooms/keys/browse carries. The outer document members (id, type, issuer, recipient, issuedAt, expiresAt, proof) are owned by the framework — SPEC §6.3.

roomId.description: The room to list. The recipient MUST already hold group state for it.

host.description: The host to list from, as a DID. Named by the caller for the same reason it is on `rooms/keys/read`: nothing maps a room to its host.

prefix.description: Restrict to keys with this prefix. Passed through to the host. **Setting it makes the listing non-comparable against the room's `recordCount`** — see `verification.count`.

sinceVersion.description: Return only records above this version. Passed through. Also makes the listing non-comparable against `recordCount`.

beforeVersion.description: Return only records whose current version is below this — an exclusive upper bound, passed through to the host's `rooms/records/list/0.8`. A surface paging a conversation backwards passes the lowest version it holds. Also makes the listing non-comparable against `recordCount`.

order.description: Passed through to the host. `oldestFirst` (the default when absent) or `newestFirst`, which reads the room's head first: with `maxPages`, the shape a member's surface uses to open a conversation at its newest messages.

limit.description: Page size to ask the host for. A cap on what a page holds, never a cap on the result: a recipient MUST follow the host's cursor to the end unless the caller asked it to stop with `maxPages`, or it stopped of its own accord, because a listing read to its end is the only one whose length means anything.

maxPages.description: The most host pages the recipient reads for this request. Absent, it reads to the end unless it stops of its own accord. A recipient that stops here with more records remaining answers `complete: false` and the host's continuation as `nextCursor`. Setting it makes the listing non-comparable against `recordCount` unless the end is reached within it.

cursor.description: A `nextCursor` from an earlier browse of the same room at the same host, with the same `prefix`, `sinceVersion`, `beforeVersion` and `order`. Passed through to the host as its listing's `cursor`; the host refuses one it did not issue or issued under another order or other bounds, and the recipient answers `hostRefused`. A listing resumed from a cursor does not start at the room's first record in its order, so it is never comparable against `recordCount`.

Response.description: Success response to rooms/keys/browse. Type https://trusttasks.org/spec/rooms/keys/browse/0.6#response.

records.description: Metadata, never bodies — the same projection the host serves, passed through. A member who wants a body asks for one record, which is also the only shape a trace can be produced for.

complete.description: Whether the recipient followed the host's cursor to the end. `false` means a page bound was hit, and is what makes `verification.count` `notComparable` even on an unfiltered listing — a short listing and a truncated one are indistinguishable by length alone, which is exactly the confusion this member exists to prevent.

nextCursor.description: The host's continuation token, present exactly when `complete` is `false`: the recipient stopped — at `maxPages` or of its own accord — while the host still had records to list. Pass it back as `cursor`, with the same `prefix`, `sinceVersion`, `beforeVersion` and `order`, to continue. Absent when the listing reached its end.

verification.description: What the recipient checked and what it found. REQUIRED for the same reason it is on `rooms/keys/read`.

lastPrune.description: The room's latest record prune, passed through from the host's listing (`rooms/records/list` 0.3) exactly as served, whenever the room's records have been pruned. A caller keeping its own copy of the room synchronised below `lastPrune.version` rebuilds it from a browse with no `sinceVersion`, as `rooms/records/list` 0.3 *After a prune* requires.

Response.title: Rooms Keys Browse — response payload

Ext.title: Ext
Ext.description: Vendor-namespaced extension object per SPEC.md §4.5.1. Each immediate key MUST be a reverse-DNS namespace; structure under each namespace is opaque to the framework.

RecordPrune.title: RecordPrune
RecordPrune.description:
The mark a prune leaves: **that** records were removed, when, and how many — never which, and never anything they said.

A prune removes records outright, tombstones included, so the room's record tree loses leaves and an incremental reader has nothing left to learn the removal from. This is what it learns from instead. A host keeps the latest one per room and serves it with every listing that can carry it (`rooms/records/list` 0.3, as `lastPrune`); a reader whose own copy of the room was synchronised to a version below `version` MUST rebuild that copy from a full listing — no `sinceVersion` — and drop every record the full listing no longer holds. Without that, a record the room removed lives on in every cache that synchronised before the prune, and a record retracted while the reader was away comes back as current.

**What a host keeps and what it does not.** A host keeps this marker, and in its audit trail the prune's `reason`, its requester where the tier discloses one, and the retention it was made under. It MUST NOT keep anything a pruned record said — body, ciphertext, cleartext, title, description, file or blob — and SHOULD NOT keep pruned records' keys: the count is the audit, and a list of keys on an `open` room, where keys may be descriptive, is content by another name.

version.description: The version the prune took from the room's counter, as a put or a curation would. No record carries it; it is what moves `HeadVersion` past the removal, so that a root taken before and a root taken after are never labelled with one version.

removed.description: How many records were removed, tombstones included. A prune that removed nothing leaves no mark.

ReadVerification.title: ReadVerification
ReadVerification.description:
What the agent checked on the member's behalf, and what it found.

**A verdict, never an error.** None of these values fails the task, including the ones that report a host caught out. A member's own agent refusing to hand over a record because the *host* misbehaved punishes the member for somebody else's act — and locks them out of the room holding the records that would show what happened, at the moment they most need them. The consequence belongs on the **write** path, where continuing to hand material to a party you have caught is what compounds the damage.

So a consumer **MUST NOT** treat any value here as a failed read, and **MUST** surface an adverse one rather than logging it. What that costs is words: a member shown a bare warning icon dismisses it, and a member later refused a write with no explanation blames their own agent. A detection the member attributes to the wrong party is worse than no detection.

Members are **absent where the task cannot produce them** rather than carrying a not-applicable value — a listing has no `trace` because there is no single record to trace, and a single read has no `count` because a count is only checkable against a listing read to its end.

trace.description:
Whether the record's `RecordTrace` reached the `dataCommitment` served beside it.

`verified` says the record is under the root the host asserted — and **nothing about whether that root is the room's**, which is what `priorRoots` and an anchor are for. `notOffered` is a host that maintains no tree, which is legal and informative. `failed` is arithmetic that does not close: the host served a path that does not reach its own root, which is either a defect or a fabrication and is not distinguishable from here.

priorRoots.description:
Whether this root matches what the agent has seen from this host for this room **at this `headVersion`**.

This is the comparison a member cannot make for themselves. A tab does not outlive itself and a CLI holds nothing; the agent is the only party on the member's side of the boundary that saw both reads.

  - `agree` — seen at this head before, same root.
  - `conflict` — seen at this head before, **different root**. A host caught: there is no write to attribute the difference to, because a write would have moved the head.
  - `noneHeld` — first read at this head. Not evidence of anything; a memory of one is not a comparison.
  - `notChecked` — this agent keeps no root history. An honest answer for an agent that cannot make the comparison, and **not** a synonym for `noneHeld`: one says nothing was found, the other says nothing was looked for.

REQUIRED, so that an agent which does not check has to say so rather than omit the question.

anchor.description:
How what the host served compares with the room's own **witnessed anchor** (`EpochAnchor`).

This is the comparison that needs neither a gossip channel rooms deliberately lack nor durable state in an agent: every member resolves the same room DID and reads the same entry, co-signed by witnesses. It is the only one of the three a first-time reader can make.

  - `agrees` — the host served the anchored state, and its root matches.
  - `ahead` — the room has moved past the anchor. The ordinary case; an anchor describes a moment, not the present, and says nothing about records written since.
  - `behind` — **the host is serving a state older than the room's own witnessed statement.** A rollback, and a detection nothing else in this family can make: a member with no history, no peer and no prior read still catches it.
  - `conflict` — same `headVersion` as the anchor, different root. The host has contradicted a value its own room published and witnesses co-signed.
  - `none` — the room has published no anchor. Not a fault; anchoring costs a witnessed update and a key rotation, and a room may reasonably decline.
  - `notChecked` — the consumer did not resolve the room. An honest answer, and **not** a synonym for `none`: one says the room published nothing, the other says nobody looked.

count.description:
Whether the number of records returned matches the `recordCount` the host committed to.

Only ever comparable against a listing with **no** `prefix`, **no** `sinceVersion` and read to its end — anything else legitimately holds fewer, and comparing it is a discrepancy the reader manufactured. `notComparable` is that case, and it is the common one.

`short` is a host contradicting itself inside one exchange: it committed to a tree of N records and served fewer, with no filter to explain the difference. That is the omission the commitment exists to make detectable, caught without a second party and without an anchor.

head.description: What the host asserted about the room, passed through unaltered so the member can compare it somewhere this agent cannot reach — with another member, or against a witnessed anchor. All three or none: a root without the state it describes is not comparable to another root, which is the whole of `HeadVersion`.

HeadVersion.title: HeadVersion
HeadVersion.description:
The highest version among the records `DataCommitment` covers. `0` for a room that holds none.

**Derived from the same set as the root, and not read from the room's own counter.** The two agree for any host that has never erased a record — versions are assigned strictly increasing and a retraction keeps its tombstone — but they are not interchangeable, because a root and a counter are *two reads*, and two reads are not a snapshot. A write landing between them yields a pair that is individually correct and jointly false: two members holding roots taken over different trees, labelled with one version. That reads as equivocation and is not, and a **false accusation discredits the mechanism rather than the host** — the worst outcome available here. Taken from the committed set, the version cannot disagree with the root it labels, whatever else is happening to the room.

**A prune is the one mutation that removes leaves, and it takes a version too.** A host that **erases** records — as distinct from retracting them, which leaves a tombstone in the tree — moves the root, and taken from the records alone this value need not move with it: it would stay put, or even fall if the erased record held the highest version, and two members straddling the erasure would see one version over two roots, which reads as equivocation and is not. So on a room whose records have been pruned (`rooms/records/prune`), this value is the higher of the highest version among the records the tree covers and the `version` of the room's latest `RecordPrune`, computed from the same snapshot as the root. A prune takes the next version from the room's counter exactly as a put or a curation does, so the pair stays a snapshot: a root and a head that agree before a prune and a root and a head that agree after it, never one head over two roots. **This is what makes two roots comparable at all**, and without it the comparison this family is built on cannot be performed. Shown two different roots, a host that equivocated and a host that was merely written to are indistinguishable — the first can always answer *the room moved between your reads*, and nothing contradicts it.

A version is assigned by exactly the mutations that change the tree — every put, curate and retraction takes the next one — so the highest of them names the **state** the root describes. DataCommitment.title: DataCommitment
DataCommitment.description:
The root of the room's record tree — a host's commitment to *which records the room holds*, as distinct from what any one of them says.

A room's records are already signed and room-bound, so a host cannot forge, alter or relocate one. What it can do for free is stay silent: a listing that omits a record is indistinguishable from a room that never held it. This value is what makes that omission detectable, so it is only worth anything when the reader can compare it against a copy the host did not choose for them — one it gave another member, one it gave the same member earlier, or the witnessed anchor. A commitment read once, in isolation, proves nothing.

**A root on its own is not comparable, and an earlier revision of this description said it was.** It claimed a host showing two members two different roots had been caught, which is false while a room can move between two reads: the host answers *there was a write*, and nothing contradicts it. Comparison needs the state each root describes, which is what `HeadVersion` names — and `RecordCount` is the other half of the same omission, since Certificate Transparency's signed tree head is a root *and a size* and this family shipped only the root. A reader that receives a `dataCommitment` **without** them can use it against a witnessed anchor, where the epoch pins the state, and **MUST NOT** compare it against another root.

**The construction is normative**, because two hosts that compute different roots over the same room make every comparison meaningless:
  1. Take every record the room holds — including tombstones, which are records — and order them by `key` using unsigned byte order.
  2. Leaf: `SHA-256(0x00 || JCS(record))`, where the record is a `CommittedRecord` — that definition fixes the members exactly, and this step used to name a *projection* instead, which two implementations could read two ways — JCS is its RFC 8785 canonicalization, and `0x00` is RFC 6962's leaf-domain prefix.
  3. Internal node: `SHA-256(0x01 || left || right)`.
  4. A level with an odd number of nodes promotes the last one unchanged. It MUST NOT be duplicated: duplicating makes a tree of n leaves collide with one of n+1 whose last is repeated, so two different rooms commit to the same root.
  5. A room holding no records commits to `SHA-256("")`, a distinguished value rather than zeroes — a root of zeroes is what an uninitialised buffer looks like, and an empty room is a real state a host must be able to commit to honestly.

The leaf covers the whole record rather than its body, and that is deliberate: a host that could flip `status` from active to retracted, move `pinned`, or rewrite `author` on an `attributed` room would rewrite what the room means without touching a byte of ciphertext. The **plaintext is never involved** — on the sealed tiers the host holds ciphertext and commits to exactly what it stores.

The commitment is over the **whole room**, never over the page being returned. A page-scoped root is one a host satisfies by construction and could never fail.

Proving that a *particular* record sits under this root is a separate question, answered by `RecordTrace` on a single-record read. A commitment catches a host that equivocates; a trace binds one record to what the host committed to. Neither is the other, and a reader wanting completeness needs both plus a root it did not get from the host it is checking.

DigestMultibase.description:
